title: Spend Bytes on Breadth: Precision–Count Trade-offs forDecode-Time KV Compression in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

paper.title: Spend Bytes on Breadth: Precision–Count Trade-offs for Decode-Time KV Compression in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
paper.abstract: Abstract Reasoning models write most of their KV cache while decoding long chains of thought (CoT), so the cache has to be compressed online under a fixed memory budget. Decode-time methods mostly decide which tokens to evict. We ask how a fixed byte budget should be split between the number of cached tokens and their precision. BreadthKV spends the bytes on more tokens at low precision, combining quantization with eviction, and picks the bit-width for each model and budget with a 60-problem end-to-end calibration, since offline attention error does not predict it reliably. On three reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, it scores above eviction alone in 17 of 18 settings and produces shorter outputs. Much of what eviction loses comes from derailed runs, which keep reasoning until the length cap without reaching an answer. On Qwen3-8B at our tightest budget, eviction sends 91% of AIME samples to the cap and BreadthKV 40%. Under the same protocol, BreadthKV is statistically indistinguishable from a joint rate–distortion allocator (RDKV) that uses 27% more KV memory-time, and it outperforms our re-implementation of ThinKV.

Long-CoT reasoning models generate 10–30K tokens per problem, and the KV cache grows with every decoded token. At 32K tokens, a single Qwen3-8B sequence holds 4.5 GiB of KV cache in bf16, so four sequences already take more memory than the model’s 16 GB of weights. The cache has to be compressed online, and there is no fixed query to guide it, as there is when compressing a prompt. Token importance also shifts during decoding, since reflection steps often return to early intermediate results, and errors accumulate over the trace. Under eviction, models can fall into loops that run until the length limit ( Chang et al., 2026b ; Cheong et al., 2026 ) , and a smaller cache can make the model write more tokens, which offsets part of the memory saved ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Recent decode-time methods decide which tokens to keep, using attention scores ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , redundancy-aware scores ( Cai et al., 2025 ) , thought-type heuristics ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) , or value ranges combined with stochastic eviction ( Chang et al., 2026b ) . Concurrent work finds that uniform random eviction, with the prompt kept, does about as well as these scores at 4 × \times compression ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . A simple offline measurement shows why the other axis, precision, deserves attention. Even an oracle that knows which tokens future queries will attend to loses about 13% of their attention mass when it keeps 10% of the tokens (§ 4 ). A long CoT keeps going back to its own intermediate results, and an evicted token cannot be recovered. A token stored at 2 bits is noisy, but a later reflection step can still find it. At a fixed byte budget, a head can keep K K tokens in fp16, about 3 ​ K 3K at 4 bits or about 6 ​ K 6K at 2 bits, so the question becomes how to trade noise per token against coverage. Zhang et al. (2025) studied this trade-off for long inputs, where pruning plus quantization beats pruning at equal memory. Long-CoT decoding differs in two ways: the cache is written during generation, so errors compound over tens of thousands of steps, and a lossy cache changes what the model writes, including how long it runs. Kim et al. (2026) compare quantization and eviction for reasoning models, but separately, and find 2-bit quantization lossy. We combine the two at equal KV bytes and much tighter budgets. On three models and four benchmarks, the byte split matters more than the token scorer. With the bit-width chosen by a short end-to-end calibration, a method we call BreadthKV, the low-bit hybrid scores above SnapKV-style eviction in 17 of 18 settings (§ 5.1 ). The best bit-width depends on the model and budget, and neither offline attention error nor a per-head online probe finds it (§ 5.2 – 5.3 ). Eviction loses mostly through derailed runs that never conclude, and keeping more tokens at lower precision makes them rarer, down to about 2 bits (§ 5.6 – 5.8 ). We also run RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) with the authors’ code, where we found and fixed a zero-point clamp in the released quantizer, and our re-implementation of ThinKV ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) under the same protocol (§ 5.4 – 5.5 ). Last, we measure the latency of an int4 decode kernel (§ 5.9 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Which tokens to keep. Most KV compression work selects tokens, and for long inputs it does so by position, accumulated attention or value-aware scores ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Sengupta et al., 2025 ) , and Ada-KV ( Feng et al., 2025 ) splits the budget across heads. Reasoning models need eviction during decoding, and a fast-growing line of methods targets that case ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2026 ; Kolawole and Smith, 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Du et al., 2026 ) . Two papers are most relevant here. Random Attention ( Wang et al., 2026b ) shows that random eviction with the prompt kept matches the scored methods at about 4 × \times compression, which suggests that better scores are not where the remaining accuracy lies. VaSE ( Chang et al., 2026b ) finds that evicting a few value states with large ranges makes generations loop, restating intermediate reasoning without progress, and names a high-precision reserve for such values as future work, which hints that precision and looping are linked. All of these methods keep the selected tokens at full precision. We fix the scorer (SnapKV-D) and vary the precision. SeerAttention-R ( Gao et al., 2025 ) learns sparse attention for long decoding but keeps the full cache, so it saves compute and not memory. How many bits. KIVI ( Liu et al., 2024 ) and KVQuant ( Hooper et al., 2024 ) quantize keys per channel and values per token, the format we use. Later work allocates bits more finely, by layer ( Li et al., 2025 ) , channel ( Xia et al., 2026 ) , token ( Boroujeni et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , query-aware channel selection for reasoning ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , or over time, as PM-KVQ ( Liu et al., 2026a ) lowers precision while a long CoT grows, and other work improves the quantizer itself ( Muller et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Chauhan et al., 2026 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ; Zandieh et al., 2025 ) . Without eviction, even a 2-bit cache of a 32K-token trace does not fit our budgets, so these methods are complementary to our question. BreadthKV uses one bit-width per model and budget, and § 5.4 tests whether finer allocation helps. Trading precision for count (closest work). More Tokens, Lower Precision ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) shows that at equal memory, pruning combined with quantization, for example 4 × \times the tokens at 4 bits, outperforms pruning alone. The study covers long-input prefill (LongBench, NIAH, RULER) on non-reasoning models, where 2-bit precision degrades sharply and about 4 bits is recommended. We study decode-time compression of long CoT, in which the cache is written during generation and a lossy cache changes how long the model runs. At our budgets, calibration picks 2 or 3 bits in 5 of 6 model–budget pairs, and always using 4 bits is significantly worse (§ 5.3 ). Not All Bits Are Equal ( Kim et al., 2026 ) compares eviction (R-KV, StreamingLLM) and quantization (HQQ, per channel) separately on Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. It counts weight memory in the budget and uses generation budgets of 2K–30K tokens and eviction budgets of 2K–8K tokens. It prefers eviction for models below the effective size of an 8-bit 4B model and finds 2-bit quantization lossy. Our 7–8B bf16 models are above that threshold, we combine quantization and eviction at equal KV bytes, and our eviction budgets (512–1024 tokens) are 2–16 × \times smaller. Joint allocators decide per token or element between several precisions and eviction. MiKV ( Yang et al., 2024b ) keeps evicted tokens at low precision, HqeKV ( Wang et al., 2026a ) lets an optimizer choose the action for each element, QEvict ( Garg et al., 2026 ) keeps full-precision, INT2 and evicted tiers at matched measured memory on long inputs, ThinKV ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) sets precision and retention by thought type, and RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) solves a joint rate–distortion allocation. ThinKV reports that hybrids trace a Pareto frontier and partly offset the length inflation of pure quantization, which reaches 5.1 × \times . These works propose allocators, whereas we vary only the byte split, with the scorer and format fixed, and evaluate ThinKV and RDKV under the same protocol. Length inflation and loops. Compression lengthens reasoning, both for KV eviction, as Hold Onto That Thought ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and ReCo ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) report, and for weight quantization ( Lian et al., 2026 ) , and Pipis et al. (2026) study why reasoning models loop in the first place. KV-Rescue ( Cheong et al., 2026 ) separates incoherent generation from repetition loops under eviction and repairs runs with reasoning steps from a small full-context model, and SkipKV ( Tian et al., 2025 ) suppresses redundant sentences. Ai et al. (2026) show that compression can keep final answers intact while degrading the reasoning behind them. Benchmarks of KV compression cover long inputs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) and reasoning ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . We add a controlled measurement of how the share of runs that reach the cap moves with the byte split (§ 5.6 ) and test whether forcing a conclusion helps (§ 5.8 ). Low-rank projection. Palu ( Chang et al., 2025 ) , xKV ( Chang et al., 2026a ) , STAR-KV ( Bhatnagar et al., 2026 ) and ShadowKV ( Sun et al., 2025 ) compress the hidden dimension. In our pilot, decode-time values are far from low-rank and their subspace drifts along the trace (§ 4 ), so we did not pursue this direction. Random Attention, QEvict, ReCo, KV-Rescue and Ai et al. (2026) appeared within three months of this work and are concurrent with it.

sections.heading: 3 Byte-budgeted precision–count compression
sections.text: Budget. For each sequence, layer and KV head, the keys and values of decode tokens are limited to the bytes of B B fp16 tokens. The prompt is kept in full and not counted, for every method. All methods compress every 128 decode steps and bring each head back to its budget. Eviction (SnapKV-D). Decode-time SnapKV keeps each head’s top- B B decode tokens by the attention they receive from the last 8 queries, max-pooled over 7 positions, and always keeps the 8 most recent tokens. R-KV, H2O, StreamingLLM and random eviction follow the same schedule with their own scores. Precision-for-count hybrid ( b b -bit + SnapKV-D). The hybrid uses the same eviction, but decode tokens older than a 128-token fp16 residual window are quantized in complete 64-token blocks in the KIVI format ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . K is quantized per channel within each 64-token group and V per token within 64-channel groups. Both use asymmetric quantization with an fp16 scale and zero point per group, which costs b + 0.5 b+0.5 bits per element. To match bytes, we raise the token budget to B b = 160 + ( B − 160 ) ⋅ 16 b + 0.5 , B_{b}=160+(B-160)\cdot\frac{16}{b+0.5}, (1) where 160 approximates the fp16 tail (128–191 tokens), so hybrids stay within about 5% of the budget; memory-time is measured exactly. Rounded down, this gives 1411/1769/2412 tokens at 4/3/2 bits at B = 512 B=512 , and 3232/4109/5689 at B = 1024 B=1024 . BreadthKV: choosing b b by end-to-end calibration. We run the byte-matched { 2 , 3 , 4 } \{2,3,4\} -bit hybrids on a held-out calibration set (60 AIME 2022–23 problems × \times 4 samples) and keep the most accurate b b for each model and budget, breaking ties toward fewer bits. Calibration takes three runs per model and budget, needs no training and uses no test problems. We call the byte-matched hybrid with the calibrated b b BreadthKV and use it as the reference in all comparisons.

sections.heading: 4 Pilot analyses
sections.text: Before running anything end to end, we checked offline whether breadth can help at all. We take teacher-forced FullKV traces of R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on 8 MATH500 problems and cut each trace at 30%, 60% and 90% of its length. At each cut, the KV of decode tokens older than the recent window is compressed to a fraction r r of its fp16 bytes, and we measure the relative error of the attention output of the next 256 queries over all layers (Table 1 ). Quantizing to 4 bits and evicting with a simple window score gives lower error than oracle eviction at every byte ratio. Eviction also has a floor that no scorer can remove. Even with exact knowledge of future attention, it loses about 13% of the future attention mass at 10% retention. Low-rank projection fits these caches poorly, since V needs 78 of its 128 dimensions to keep 90% of its energy, and its top-16 subspace drifts between the first and last thirds of a trace (overlap 0.69). sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Setup. We evaluate R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, R1-Distill-Llama-8B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We report pass@1 on AIME24 and AIME25 with 8 samples per problem, on MATH500 with one sample, and on GPQA-Diamond with 4 samples (R1-Qwen only). We decode with temperature 0.6 and top- p p 0.95 (top- k k 20 for Qwen3), up to 32K tokens (16K for MATH500), at budgets B ∈ { 512 , 1024 } B\in\{512,1024\} . AIME24 with R1-Qwen served as our dev set while we developed the methods (Appendix B ), so we exclude it from the test results. For statistics, we use a paired bootstrap over problems (5000 resamples, 95% CI); pooled tests over settings resample problems within each setting. We use our own decoding engine on HF weights, with FlashAttention-2 decoding ( Dao, 2024 ) , CUDA graphs and per-head variable-length caches. The engine matches HF (teacher-forced top-1 agreement ≥ \geq 98%) and reproduces the reported FullKV accuracy of R1-Qwen (MATH500 93.0 vs. 92.8; AIME24 55.4 vs. 55.5). Appendix A gives prompts, grading, data sources, software and compute, and Appendix C lists the results for every setting.

sections.heading: 5.2 The best bit-width depends on budget and model
sections.text: No single bit-width is best everywhere. On our dev set, the best width shared by all heads rises with the budget, from 2 bits at B = 256 B=256 to 8 bits at B = 2048 B=2048 (Appendix B ). On the test sets the preference depends on the model. For the R1-Distill models, the 2-, 3- and 4-bit hybrids are close at B = 1024 B=1024 , while Qwen3-8B clearly prefers 2 bits (Table 9 ). Qwen3-8B also writes the longest AIME traces (15.5–18.5K tokens on average, against 13–14K for the R1-Distill models). This fits the idea that longer traces need more coverage, but with three models we cannot separate trace length from other differences between them. Per-head online allocation did not help. Our first approach chose the width online for each head (PACT, Appendix B ). Offline, letting each head pick its own width lowers attention error by 20–42%, and a cheap probe on recent queries recovers most of that gain, but end to end the per-head version scored below a fixed 4-bit width on the dev set and was indistinguishable from fixed widths on the test sets (1 of 18 comparisons significant). A width table tuned on the dev set did not transfer either; on Qwen3-8B it trails the 2-bit hybrid in all six AIME and MATH500 settings. More generally, attention error at a single step predicts accuracy poorly. Random eviction, for example, has 1.8 × \times the attention error of window-based eviction and the same dev accuracy. sections.heading: 5.3 Choosing the bit-width by end-to-end calibration
sections.text: Since neither offline error nor online probes find the best width, we measure it directly. Offline distortion curves at equal bytes, computed on 6 FullKV AIME24 traces per model (not used to choose b b ), get the preference wrong on two of the three models; for Qwen3-8B they favor 4 over 2 bits, the opposite of what happens end to end. Three calibration runs per model and budget pick the widths in Table 4 , and Table 4 and Fig. 3 show how the choice does on the 18 held-out settings. Calibration beats always using 4 bits by 4.5 pp pooled [+3.2, +5.8] and always using 3 bits by 2.1 pp [+1.2, +3.1]. It is not significantly better than always using 2 bits (+0.4 pp [ − 0.2 -0.2 , +1.0]). Calibration matters because each fixed width does badly on some model, 2 bits on R1-Llama (mean regret 3.1 pp) and 4 bits on Qwen3 (12.7 pp), while calibration stays within 1.3 pp on every model. On Qwen3, where a wrong choice hurts most, the choice is also stable. Resampling the calibration problems picks 2 bits in 100% and 99% of resamples at the two budgets. sections.heading: 5.4 Comparison with a joint rate–distortion allocator (RDKV)
sections.text: RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) is the prior method closest to our view of trading precision for count, so we reproduce it with the authors’ code. It treats eviction and quantization as one rate–distortion problem. For each KV head, a Lagrangian knapsack assigns each V token and each K channel a width in { 0 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } \{0,2,4,8,16\} bits, where 0 means the token is evicted or the channel is pruned, and weights a calibrated distortion table ϵ ⁡ ( b ) \epsilon(b) by attention-based importance. Reproduction. The released code compresses the prompt once after prefill and provides a block-wise mode for decoding, which we use. Decode tokens are grouped into 128-token blocks. When the next block is complete, a block is scored with the queries of that next block, allocated once by the same knapsack under a per-block budget of b b fp16-token equivalents, and then frozen. We call the upstream scoring, knapsack solver and ϵ \epsilon calibration directly, and run the calibration on traces from our calibration set. A unit test checks that our batched allocation matches upstream _perhead_select_and_pack bit for bit. Because the block mode has no total budget, we choose b b for each model and budget so that RDKV’s mean KV memory-time on the calibration set matches that of BreadthKV. This gives b = 4 b=4 at B = 512 B=512 and b = 13 / 15 / 11 b=13/15/11 at B = 1024 B=1024 for R1-Qwen/R1-Llama/Qwen3. As for all methods, the prompt is kept in full. The released quantizer clamps the zero point. The released quantize_and_pack sets the zero point to clamp ( round ( − min / s ) , 0 , 2 b − 1 ) \mathrm{clamp}(\mathrm{round}(-\min/s),0,2^{b}-1) , which clips groups whose range does not contain 0. Post-RoPE low-frequency K channels often keep the same sign throughout a 128-token block. For such channels, even the 8-bit K error is 0.3–0.45 instead of ≈ \approx 0.004, and generation degenerates. In the prefill setting the code was written for, a channel spans thousands of tokens and its range almost always contains 0, which probably hid the issue. Our fix stores the minimum as the offset and uses the same bits and metadata. With the released quantizer, RDKV scores 5–13 pp below the fixed version on AIME25 for R1-Qwen and Qwen3 and collapses on R1-Llama at both budgets (0.0% vs. 31.7/35.8%, with 73/57% of samples capped). All other RDKV results use the fixed quantizer. sections.heading: 5.5 Comparison with thought-adaptive compression (ThinKV)
sections.text: ThinKV ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) uses attention sparsity to classify segments of the CoT as reasoning (R), execution (E) or transition (T) thoughts, and quantizes each type at its own precision. The R4E4T2 setting uses NVFP4 for R and E and ternary values for T, in groups of 16 with FP8 scales. At every transition, ThinKV anneals each earlier segment from 128 to 64, …, 4 tokens, keeping tokens chosen by K-means on the keys. No code is available, so we re-implemented it from the paper, converting its token budget to our byte budget and keeping the prompt in full. Reproduction choices. The paper leaves open the ternary quantizer (we use TWN), the K-means initialization (we run 8 Lloyd iterations), and how a segment’s sparsity is aggregated (we take the mean over its steps). On our models, the paper’s KDE calibration rarely finds three sparsity modes (at most 1 of 24 traces per layer), so the thresholds fall back to tertiles. Thresholds computed offline on FullKV traces also do not transfer to decoding under compression, because sparsity depends on the number of cached entries. With offline thresholds, 61–100% of runtime segments fall into a single type (at least 97% at B = 512 B=512 ) and almost none into transitions. So we set the thresholds at the tertiles of ThinKV’s own runtime sparsity on the calibration set, iterating twice. sections.heading: 5.6 Runs that reach the length cap
sections.text: Most of what eviction loses on R1-Llama and Qwen3 comes from runs that never finish. We call a run derailed if it reaches the 32K cap. Derailed runs are almost never correct (at most 10 of 240–480 samples per configuration are both derailed and correct), and on these two models 74–98% of SnapKV-D’s wrong answers are derailed (Table 7 ; Fig. 4 ). On R1-Qwen, derailment accounts for a smaller share of the errors, and compression also lowers accuracy on runs that finish; on the same problems, finished SnapKV-D runs at B = 512 B=512 score 21.9% against 42.5% for FullKV. Appendix D shows one from Qwen3-8B with SnapKV-D at B = 512 B=512 , on an AIME24 problem that FullKV and both hybrids solve in all 8 samples. The run finds the right conditional probability within the first tenth of its output and then checks it again and again, in slightly different words each time, until it is cut off at 32K tokens without closing its reasoning. We suspect the following mechanism, although we have not tested it directly. A long CoT keeps returning to its own intermediate results. Under eviction, a result that has not been attended to for a while is dropped, and so is the record that it was already verified. When the model later wants to rely on it, it finds nothing to build on and derives it again, and that derivation is itself evicted a few thousand tokens later. A low-bit cache keeps several times as many tokens. They are noisy, but the model can still see that the check was done and move on. The frequency of “wait” is consistent with this. On Qwen3 AIME24 at B = 512 B=512 , SnapKV-D runs contain 6.4 “wait”s per thousand tokens, against 5.0 for the 2-bit hybrid and 3.7 for FullKV. A direct test would track whether the tokens of an earlier check are still in the cache when the model starts a new one. At equal bytes, fewer bits per token do mean fewer derailed runs. Going from 4 to 3 to 2 bits never raises the capped share, and 2 bits is below 4 bits in all six model–budget pairs. Fewer derailed runs do not always mean higher accuracy, because fewer bits also add noise to every retained token. On R1-Llama at B = 512 B=512 , 4 bits derails about twice as often as 2 bits and still scores higher.

sections.heading: 5.7 The floor of breadth: sub-2-bit and rotated codecs
sections.text: To test whether breadth still helps below 2 bits, we use TurboQuant-style codecs ( LM-c ), which combine a random-sign Hadamard rotation, a per-token fp16 norm and Gaussian Lloyd–Max levels, and remove K’s per-channel mean in each 64-token group. LM-c2 costs 2.25 bits per element (KIVI-2 costs 2.5), and LM-c1 costs 1.25. Offline, LM-c makes 1 bit usable, with attention errors of 0.27–0.40 against 2.2–5.1 for uniform 1-bit quantization, and LM-c2 matches KIVI-2’s error with 10% fewer bytes. End to end, none of them helps, and with these codecs the benefit of breadth ends at about 2 bits. LM-c1 collapses, with 0–12% calibration accuracy and 73–100% of samples capped (we stopped these runs early once this was clear), and pairing KIVI-2 keys with 1-bit LM values (1.81 bits) is much worse than KIVI-2 on Qwen3. Over the 18 test settings, LM-c2 is 2.6 pp below the KIVI-2 hybrid at equal bytes [ − 3.8 -3.8 , − 1.4 -1.4 ], writes 11% longer outputs and derails more in all six AIME configurations, although its offline error is the same. Whatever makes the difference, the averaged single-step error we measure does not see it. The calibration set would have rejected LM-c2 for Qwen3, but it favored LM-c2 on the R1 models by 2.5–3.3 pp, a gain that did not hold on the test sets.

sections.heading: 5.8 Can derailed runs be rescued after the fact?
sections.text: Since derailed runs fail by never concluding, we tested on the calibration set whether forcing a conclusion helps; it mostly does not. For each capped run of the 2-bit hybrid, we cut the run at the loop onset found by an n n -gram repetition detector (24-grams, ≥ \geq 60% repeated within a 1K window); if the detector finds no onset, we drop the last 4K tokens instead. We then append </think> and let the model answer under the same compressed cache (Table 8 ). This recovers 15% of capped runs on Qwen3 and almost none on the R1 models, below the 30% we had set in advance as the bar for running it on the test sets. Part of the problem is the detector, which almost never fires on finished runs but finds an onset in only 6 of 115 and 8 of 51 capped Qwen3 runs, because most derailed runs repeat reasoning steps and not long exact spans, as in Appendix D . sections.heading: 5.9 Efficiency
sections.text: To see whether low-bit storage slows decoding, we implement a Triton split-K decode kernel that reads packed low-bit KV directly. Codes are stored in a planar layout, so unpacking is a shift and a mask; dot products run in fp16 on tensor cores, and the V rotation is undone once on the output. The kernel stores K as in the hybrids and V with one scale/zero pair per token instead of two (the layout of Appendix B ), and its maximum relative error against a PyTorch reference is 0.7%. On an H200 (batch 64, R1-Qwen-7B heads, one layer, one decode step) at 32K context, fp16 FlashAttention takes 1.63 ms and int8/int4/int2 take 2.35/1.70/2.21 ms; at 16K, the times are 0.75 and 1.20/0.87/1.13 ms. Int4 is close to fp16 latency at 27% of the memory, so a fixed memory could hold about 3.7 × \times (int4) to 6.7 × \times (int2) more sequences. The kernel is compute-bound, because the 7 query heads per KV head are padded to 16 MMA rows, and int2 is not faster than int4.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: For decode-time compression of long CoT, how a byte budget is split between tokens and precision mattered more in our experiments than which tokens an eviction method keeps. Spending the bytes on more low-bit tokens, with the bit-width set by a short end-to-end calibration, beat eviction in 17 of 18 settings and matched a joint rate–distortion allocator that uses more memory. Offline attention error and per-head probes did not identify the bit-width, so we would not set it without an end-to-end run. The open problem is derailment on long traces. On Qwen3-8B, 40% of 2-bit runs at our tightest budget still reach the cap, and forcing a conclusion recovers few of them. If our account of derailment is right, a cache that keeps even a coarse record of what the model has already checked should help more than a better token scorer.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Calibration. The calibration set is small and was validated at two budgets. At these budgets, always using 2 bits is statistically on par with calibration. The benefit of calibration is that it avoids the model-specific failures of other fixed choices; whether it is needed at larger budgets has not been tested on held-out data. Statistical power. AIME has 30 problems per year, so single-setting confidence intervals are wide. Cross-setting claims rest on pooled tests. Each configuration uses one sampling seed; variance across seeds is covered only through repeated samples per problem and is not reported separately. Models, tasks and languages. We study three open 7–8B reasoning models (two R1-distilled, one Qwen3) on English mathematics and science benchmarks; GPQA was run on one model only. We did not evaluate code generation, long-input tasks, other languages, larger models or other reasoning-model families, so the breadth–depth trade-off and the calibrated bit-widths may differ there. Mechanism. The derailment analysis is correlational, and the mechanism in § 5.6 is a hypothesis we have not tested. The rescue experiment used a literal-repetition detector, ran on calibration data only and intervened late. Reproduced baselines. RDKV’s decode mode has no total budget, so its memory is matched only approximately, and we modified the zero point of its quantizer (we also report as-released results). ThinKV has no public code; our re-implementation fixes details the paper leaves open, calibrates thresholds on runtime sparsity and adds K-channel centering, whose per-segment means our byte count only partly charges (we report a bound). Results from the authors’ own implementations may differ. Scope of the comparisons. The sub-2-bit study covers one codec family; vector or learned codebooks might move the floor. The low-rank baseline uses a frozen basis. We did not run every recent reasoning-specific method; R-KV represents reasoning-aware eviction. Simulated quantization. Quantization is simulated in the engine (quantize, then dequantize) with exact byte accounting. We do not measure end-to-end memory or serving throughput; the sequence counts in § 5.9 are a projection from the kernel, which uses a closely related but not identical layout. Test contamination. Some benchmarks, MATH500 in particular, may appear in the models’ training data. All comparisons are between compression methods on the same model, so contamination should affect absolute accuracy more than the differences we report, but we cannot rule out interactions.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This work studies inference efficiency and poses low direct risk. Compression can preserve final answers while degrading the reasoning that supports them ( Ai et al., 2026 ) , so compressed reasoning models should be evaluated beyond final-answer accuracy before deployment. We use publicly released models and benchmarks for evaluation only, consistent with their intended research use. The DeepSeek-R1-Distill models are MIT-licensed (the Llama-based one is also subject to the Llama 3.1 license), Qwen3-8B is under Apache 2.0, GPQA under CC BY 4.0 and MATH under MIT, and the AIME problems are published by the MAA; we use public copies on Hugging Face. The RDKV code is MIT-licensed. The benchmarks contain no personal data. Use of AI assistants. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to write most of the code (the decoding engine, compression methods, baseline reproductions, kernel and analysis scripts), to run and monitor experiments, to search the literature and to draft the text. Every reported number is computed by scripts from logged generations. The author takes full responsibility for the content.

sections.heading: Appendix A Experimental Details
sections.text: Prompts. Each problem is sent as a single user turn through the model’s chat template (Qwen3 with thinking enabled), followed by “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{} .” For GPQA the suffix asks for the letter of the correct option (A–D) within \boxed{} ; each question lists its four options as lettered choices. Grading. We take the last \boxed{} after </think> (or anywhere in the output if the answer region has none). Math answers are compared with math-verify (0.9.0), falling back to exact string match after removing spaces; GPQA answers are compared by option letter. Runs that hit the length cap without an answer count as wrong. Data. MATH500 (500 problems), AIME 2024 and 2025 (30 each) and GPQA-Diamond (198) are loaded from Hugging Face copies. The calibration set is the 60 AIME 2022–2023 problems of the AIMO validation set, disjoint from all test sets. Engine and software. Models run in bf16 in our own decoding engine (FlashAttention-2 decode, CUDA graphs, per-head variable-length caches) with PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.56.2, FlashAttention 2.8.3 and Triton 3.4.0. Generation runs used H200 and A800 GPUs and took about 344 GPU-hours in total, excluding offline analyses. Eviction details. SnapKV-D scores decode tokens by the attention of the last 8 queries, max-pooled with kernel 7, and always keeps the 8 most recent tokens. All methods compress every 128 decode steps.

sections.heading: Appendix B PACT: Per-Head Online Allocation
sections.text: PACT was our first attempt to choose the bit-width online, separately for each KV head. It is a negative result, and we report it here for completeness. Format and selection. PACT uses the hybrids’ K format, with V quantized per token in a Hadamard-rotated basis ( b + 0.25 b+0.25 bits); quantizing K per token gives a relative attention error of 1.92 at layer 0 at 2 bits, even after rotation. At each compression step, a head keeps its top- K b K_{b} tokens by attention from the last 32 queries, stored at b b bits, where K b K_{b} is the number of tokens the budget can hold at that width. Variants. PACT-B reads b b from a budget-indexed table chosen on the dev set (512 → \to 3, 1024 → \to 4, 2048 → \to 8). PACT-LA tries each b ∈ { 16 , 8 , 4 , 3 , 2 } b\in\{16,8,4,3,2\} that is not above the head’s current width, measures the relative change in the attention output of the last 32 queries (the probe), and picks the b b with the smallest change, evaluating each b b at the number of tokens it could keep once the history has grown by a factor of γ = 4 \gamma=4 . A head’s precision never increases. Without this look-ahead, the probe picks 8 bits for 88% of heads and inflates output lengths. Offline motivation. With per-token-independent quantization on the pilot traces, letting each head choose its own bit-width lowers attention error by 20–42% relative to the best single width shared by all heads, and a probe on the last 64 queries recovers 90–95% of this per-head oracle gain. Dev results (R1-Qwen AIME24). With one width for all heads, the best width rises with the budget, from 2 bits at B = 256 B=256 (26.2%) to 3 bits at 512 (46.2%, against 40.0% at 4 bits), 4 bits at 1024 (54.2%) and 8 bits at 2048 (54.6%). At B = 1024 B=1024 , PACT-LA scores 52.5%, PACT-LA with γ = 2 \gamma=2 49.6%, and the probe without look-ahead 46.7% with 16.2% of samples capped, all below the fixed 4-bit width. Test results. PACT-LA and PACT-B differ significantly in 1 of 18 test comparisons. On Qwen3-8B, PACT-B’s table (3 or 4 bits) trails the 2-bit hybrid in all six AIME and MATH500 settings ( − 2.0 -2.0 to − 18.8 -18.8 pp, 5 significant), and on R1-Qwen AIME25 at B = 2048 B=2048 its 8 bits (34.2%) trail the 4-bit hybrid (37.9%).

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.05685v1 [cs.CL] 05 Oct 2026 Spend Bytes on Breadth: Precision–Count Trade-offs for Decode-Time KV Compression in Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Runguo Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Email: runguol2@illinois.edu Abstract Reasoning models write most of their KV cache while decoding long chains of thought (CoT), so the cache has to be compressed online under a fixed memory budget. Decode-time methods mostly decide which tokens to evict. We ask how a fixed byte budget should be split between the number of cached tokens and their precision. BreadthKV spends the bytes on more tokens at low precision, combining quantization with eviction, and picks the bit-width for each model and budget with a 60-problem end-to-end calibration, since offline attention error does not predict it reliably. On three reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, it scores above eviction alone in 17 of 18 settings and produces shorter outputs. Much of what eviction loses comes from derailed runs, which keep reasoning until the length cap without reaching an answer. On Qwen3-8B at our tightest budget, eviction sends 91% of AIME samples to the cap and BreadthKV 40%. Under the same protocol, BreadthKV is statistically indistinguishable from a joint rate–distortion allocator (RDKV) that uses 27% more KV memory-time, and it outperforms our re-implementation of ThinKV. 1 Introduction (a) Same bytes, different split (one KV head, at a compression step) decode-token budget: bytes of B B fp16 tokens Eviction (SnapKV-D) prompt (fp16) × \times × \times × \times × \times × \times × \times × \times B B = 512 tokens, 16-bit evicted BreadthKV prompt (fp16) × \times × \times B b B_{b} tokens at b b bits (KIVI format: K per channel, V per token) fp16 window B = 512 B=512 , b = 2 b=2 : B b = 2,412 B_{b}=2{,}412 tokens Every 128 decode steps: ① quantize full 64-token blocks outside the 128-token fp16 window; ② evict with SnapKV-D to B b = 160 + ( B − 160 ) ⋅ 16 / ( b + 0.5 ) B_{b}=160+(B-160)\cdot 16/(b+0.5) tokens. (a) At the same KV byte budget per head, eviction keeps B B full-precision decode tokens, whereas BreadthKV quantizes older tokens to b b bits in the KIVI format and keeps B b B_{b} of them plus a 128-token fp16 window; both compress every 128 decode steps and keep the prompt in full. (b) The bit-width is chosen for each model and budget by running the byte-matched { 2 , 3 , 4 } \{2,3,4\} -bit hybrids on 60 held-out AIME problems. (c) At equal bytes, fewer bits per token lower the share of runs that reach the 32K cap and raise accuracy (FullKV: 10.2% capped, 69.8% accuracy). Squares are not to scale. Long-CoT reasoning models generate 10–30K tokens per problem, and the KV cache grows with every decoded token. At 32K tokens, a single Qwen3-8B sequence holds 4.5 GiB of KV cache in bf16, so four sequences already take more memory than the model’s 16 GB of weights. The cache has to be compressed online, and there is no fixed query to guide it, as there is when compressing a prompt. Token importance also shifts during decoding, since reflection steps often return to early intermediate results, and errors accumulate over the trace. Under eviction, models can fall into loops that run until the length limit ( Chang et al., 2026b ; Cheong et al., 2026 ) , and a smaller cache can make the model write more tokens, which offsets part of the memory saved ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . Recent decode-time methods decide which tokens to keep, using attention scores ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) , redundancy-aware scores ( Cai et al., 2025 ) , thought-type heuristics ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) , or value ranges combined with stochastic eviction ( Chang et al., 2026b ) . Concurrent work finds that uniform random eviction, with the prompt kept, does about as well as these scores at 4 × \times compression ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . A simple offline measurement shows why the other axis, precision, deserves attention. Even an oracle that knows which tokens future queries will attend to loses about 13% of their attention mass when it keeps 10% of the tokens (§ 4 ). A long CoT keeps going back to its own intermediate results, and an evicted token cannot be recovered. A token stored at 2 bits is noisy, but a later reflection step can still find it. At a fixed byte budget, a head can keep K K tokens in fp16, about 3 ​ K 3K at 4 bits or about 6 ​ K 6K at 2 bits, so the question becomes how to trade noise per token against coverage. Zhang et al. (2025) studied this trade-off for long inputs, where pruning plus quantization beats pruning at equal memory. Long-CoT decoding differs in two ways: the cache is written during generation, so errors compound over tens of thousands of steps, and a lossy cache changes what the model writes, including how long it runs. Kim et al. (2026) compare quantization and eviction for reasoning models, but separately, and find 2-bit quantization lossy. We combine the two at equal KV bytes and much tighter budgets. On three models and four benchmarks, the byte split matters more than the token scorer. With the bit-width chosen by a short end-to-end calibration, a method we call BreadthKV, the low-bit hybrid scores above SnapKV-style eviction in 17 of 18 settings (§ 5.1 ). The best bit-width depends on the model and budget, and neither offline attention error nor a per-head online probe finds it (§ 5.2 – 5.3 ). Eviction loses mostly through derailed runs that never conclude, and keeping more tokens at lower precision makes them rarer, down to about 2 bits (§ 5.6 – 5.8 ). We also run RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) with the authors’ code, where we found and fixed a zero-point clamp in the released quantizer, and our re-implementation of ThinKV ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) under the same protocol (§ 5.4 – 5.5 ). Last, we measure the latency of an int4 decode kernel (§ 5.9 ). 2 Related work Which tokens to keep. Most KV compression work selects tokens, and for long inputs it does so by position, accumulated attention or value-aware scores ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Sengupta et al., 2025 ) , and Ada-KV ( Feng et al., 2025 ) splits the budget across heads. Reasoning models need eviction during decoding, and a fast-growing line of methods targets that case ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2026 ; Kolawole and Smith, 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Du et al., 2026 ) . Two papers are most relevant here. Random Attention ( Wang et al., 2026b ) shows that random eviction with the prompt kept matches the scored methods at about 4 × \times compression, which suggests that better scores are not where the remaining accuracy lies. VaSE ( Chang et al., 2026b ) finds that evicting a few value states with large ranges makes generations loop, restating intermediate reasoning without progress, and names a high-precision reserve for such values as future work, which hints that precision and looping are linked. All of these methods keep the selected tokens at full precision. We fix the scorer (SnapKV-D) and vary the precision. SeerAttention-R ( Gao et al., 2025 ) learns sparse attention for long decoding but keeps the full cache, so it saves compute and not memory. How many bits. KIVI ( Liu et al., 2024 ) and KVQuant ( Hooper et al., 2024 ) quantize keys per channel and values per token, the format we use. Later work allocates bits more finely, by layer ( Li et al., 2025 ) , channel ( Xia et al., 2026 ) , token ( Boroujeni et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , query-aware channel selection for reasoning ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , or over time, as PM-KVQ ( Liu et al., 2026a ) lowers precision while a long CoT grows, and other work improves the quantizer itself ( Muller et al., 2026 ; Zuo et al., 2026 ; Chauhan et al., 2026 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ; Zandieh et al., 2025 ) . Without eviction, even a 2-bit cache of a 32K-token trace does not fit our budgets, so these methods are complementary to our question. BreadthKV uses one bit-width per model and budget, and § 5.4 tests whether finer allocation helps. Trading precision for count (closest work). More Tokens, Lower Precision ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) shows that at equal memory, pruning combined with quantization, for example 4 × \times the tokens at 4 bits, outperforms pruning alone. The study covers long-input prefill (LongBench, NIAH, RULER) on non-reasoning models, where 2-bit precision degrades sharply and about 4 bits is recommended. We study decode-time compression of long CoT, in which the cache is written during generation and a lossy cache changes how long the model runs. At our budgets, calibration picks 2 or 3 bits in 5 of 6 model–budget pairs, and always using 4 bits is significantly worse (§ 5.3 ). Not All Bits Are Equal ( Kim et al., 2026 ) compares eviction (R-KV, StreamingLLM) and quantization (HQQ, per channel) separately on Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. It counts weight memory in the budget and uses generation budgets of 2K–30K tokens and eviction budgets of 2K–8K tokens. It prefers eviction for models below the effective size of an 8-bit 4B model and finds 2-bit quantization lossy. Our 7–8B bf16 models are above that threshold, we combine quantization and eviction at equal KV bytes, and our eviction budgets (512–1024 tokens) are 2–16 × \times smaller. Joint allocators decide per token or element between several precisions and eviction. MiKV ( Yang et al., 2024b ) keeps evicted tokens at low precision, HqeKV ( Wang et al., 2026a ) lets an optimizer choose the action for each element, QEvict ( Garg et al., 2026 ) keeps full-precision, INT2 and evicted tiers at matched measured memory on long inputs, ThinKV ( Ramachandran et al., 2026 ) sets precision and retention by thought type, and RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) solves a joint rate–distortion allocation. ThinKV reports that hybrids trace a Pareto frontier and partly offset the length inflation of pure quantization, which reaches 5.1 × \times . These works propose allocators, whereas we vary only the byte split, with the scorer and format fixed, and evaluate ThinKV and RDKV under the same protocol. Length inflation and loops. Compression lengthens reasoning, both for KV eviction, as Hold Onto That Thought ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and ReCo ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) report, and for weight quantization ( Lian et al., 2026 ) , and Pipis et al. (2026) study why reasoning models loop in the first place. KV-Rescue ( Cheong et al., 2026 ) separates incoherent generation from repetition loops under eviction and repairs runs with reasoning steps from a small full-context model, and SkipKV ( Tian et al., 2025 ) suppresses redundant sentences. Ai et al. (2026) show that compression can keep final answers intact while degrading the reasoning behind them. Benchmarks of KV compression cover long inputs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) and reasoning ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . We add a controlled measurement of how the share of runs that reach the cap moves with the byte split (§ 5.6 ) and test whether forcing a conclusion helps (§ 5.8 ). Low-rank projection. Palu ( Chang et al., 2025 ) , xKV ( Chang et al., 2026a ) , STAR-KV ( Bhatnagar et al., 2026 ) and ShadowKV ( Sun et al., 2025 ) compress the hidden dimension. In our pilot, decode-time values are far from low-rank and their subspace drifts along the trace (§ 4 ), so we did not pursue this direction. Random Attention, QEvict, ReCo, KV-Rescue and Ai et al. (2026) appeared within three months of this work and are concurrent with it. 3 Byte-budgeted precision–count compression Budget. For each sequence, layer and KV head, the keys and values of decode tokens are limited to the bytes of B B fp16 tokens. The prompt is kept in full and not counted, for every method. All methods compress every 128 decode steps and bring each head back to its budget. Eviction (SnapKV-D). Decode-time SnapKV keeps each head’s top- B B decode tokens by the attention they receive from the last 8 queries, max-pooled over 7 positions, and always keeps the 8 most recent tokens. R-KV, H2O, StreamingLLM and random eviction follow the same schedule with their own scores. Precision-for-count hybrid ( b b -bit + SnapKV-D). The hybrid uses the same eviction, but decode tokens older than a 128-token fp16 residual window are quantized in complete 64-token blocks in the KIVI format ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . K is quantized per channel within each 64-token group and V per token within 64-channel groups. Both use asymmetric quantization with an fp16 scale and zero point per group, which costs b + 0.5 b+0.5 bits per element. To match bytes, we raise the token budget to B b = 160 + ( B − 160 ) ⋅ 16 b + 0.5 , B_{b}=160+(B-160)\cdot\frac{16}{b+0.5}, (1) where 160 approximates the fp16 tail (128–191 tokens), so hybrids stay within about 5% of the budget; memory-time is measured exactly. Rounded down, this gives 1411/1769/2412 tokens at 4/3/2 bits at B = 512 B=512 , and 3232/4109/5689 at B = 1024 B=1024 . BreadthKV: choosing b b by end-to-end calibration. We run the byte-matched { 2 , 3 , 4 } \{2,3,4\} -bit hybrids on a held-out calibration set (60 AIME 2022–23 problems × \times 4 samples) and keep the most accurate b b for each model and budget, breaking ties toward fewer bits. Calibration takes three runs per model and budget, needs no training and uses no test problems. We call the byte-matched hybrid with the calibrated b b BreadthKV and use it as the reference in all comparisons. 4 Pilot analyses Before running anything end to end, we checked offline whether breadth can help at all. We take teacher-forced FullKV traces of R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on 8 MATH500 problems and cut each trace at 30%, 60% and 90% of its length. At each cut, the KV of decode tokens older than the recent window is compressed to a fraction r r of its fp16 bytes, and we measure the relative error of the attention output of the next 256 queries over all layers (Table 1 ). Quantizing to 4 bits and evicting with a simple window score gives lower error than oracle eviction at every byte ratio. Eviction also has a floor that no scorer can remove. Even with exact knowledge of future attention, it loses about 13% of the future attention mass at 10% retention. Low-rank projection fits these caches poorly, since V needs 78 of its 128 dimensions to keep 90% of its energy, and its top-16 subspace drifts between the first and last thirds of a trace (overlap 0.69). We evaluate R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, R1-Distill-Llama-8B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We report pass@1 on AIME24 and AIME25 with 8 samples per problem, on MATH500 with one sample, and on GPQA-Diamond with 4 samples (R1-Qwen only). We decode with temperature 0.6 and top- p p 0.95 (top- k k 20 for Qwen3), up to 32K tokens (16K for MATH500), at budgets B ∈ { 512 , 1024 } B\in\{512,1024\} . AIME24 with R1-Qwen served as our dev set while we developed the methods (Appendix B ), so we exclude it from the test results. For statistics, we use a paired bootstrap over problems (5000 resamples, 95% CI); pooled tests over settings resample problems within each setting. We use our own decoding engine on HF weights, with FlashAttention-2 decoding ( Dao, 2024 ) , CUDA graphs and per-head variable-length caches. The engine matches HF (teacher-forced top-1 agreement ≥ \geq 98%) and reproduces the reported FullKV accuracy of R1-Qwen (MATH500 93.0 vs. 92.8; AIME24 55.4 vs. 55.5). Appendix A gives prompts, grading, data sources, software and compute, and Appendix C lists the results for every setting. 5.1 Main results Figure 2: Accuracy vs. KV memory-time (relative to FullKV) on AIME25. Each line connects a method’s results at B = 512 B=512 and 1024; upper left is better. BreadthKV uses the calibrated bit-width, so its points coincide with the hybrid of that width where one is plotted (on Qwen3-8B it covers the 2-bit line). The square is KIVI-4 without eviction, and the dashed line is FullKV. Keeping more tokens at low precision beats keeping fewer tokens in fp16, and on Qwen3-8B the difference is large. Table 2 gives BreadthKV’s gain over SnapKV-D at the same budget. The gain is positive in 17 of 18 settings, its CI excludes zero in 16, and pooled over all settings it is 17.4 pp [15.6, 19.3]. The one negative case is R1-Llama MATH500 at B = 1024 B=1024 , where SnapKV-D is already within 2.4 pp of FullKV. It treats eviction and quantization as one rate–distortion problem. For each KV head, a Lagrangian knapsack assigns each V token and each K channel a width in { 0 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 } \{0,2,4,8,16\} bits, where 0 means the token is evicted or the channel is pruned, and weights a calibrated distortion table ϵ ⁡ ( b ) \epsilon(b) by attention-based importance. When the next block is complete, a block is scored with the queries of that next block, allocated once by the same knapsack under a per-block budget of b b fp16-token equivalents, and then frozen. We call the upstream scoring, knapsack solver and ϵ \epsilon calibration directly, and run the calibration on traces from our calibration set. A unit test checks that our batched allocation matches upstream _perhead_select_and_pack bit for bit. Because the block mode has no total budget, we choose b b for each model and budget so that RDKV’s mean KV memory-time on the calibration set matches that of BreadthKV. No code is available, so we re-implemented it from the paper, converting its token budget to our byte budget and keeping the prompt in full. Reproduction choices. The paper leaves open the ternary quantizer (we use TWN), the K-means initialization (we run 8 Lloyd iterations), and how a segment’s sparsity is aggregated (we take the mean over its steps). On our models, the paper’s KDE calibration rarely finds three sparsity modes (at most 1 of 24 traces per layer), so the thresholds fall back to tertiles. Thresholds computed offline on FullKV traces also do not transfer to decoding under compression, because sparsity depends on the number of cached entries. With offline thresholds, 61–100% of runtime segments fall into a single type (at least 97% at B = 512 B=512 ) and almost none into transitions. So we set the thresholds at the tertiles of ThinKV’s own runtime sparsity on the calibration set, iterating twice. LM-c2 costs 2.25 bits per element (KIVI-2 costs 2.5), and LM-c1 costs 1.25. Offline, LM-c makes 1 bit usable, with attention errors of 0.27–0.40 against 2.2–5.1 for uniform 1-bit quantization, and LM-c2 matches KIVI-2’s error with 10% fewer bytes. End to end, none of them helps, and with these codecs the benefit of breadth ends at about 2 bits. LM-c1 collapses, with 0–12% calibration accuracy and 73–100% of samples capped (we stopped these runs early once this was clear), and pairing KIVI-2 keys with 1-bit LM values (1.81 bits) is much worse than KIVI-2 on Qwen3. Over the 18 test settings, LM-c2 is 2.6 pp below the KIVI-2 hybrid at equal bytes [ − 3.8 -3.8 , − 1.4 -1.4 ], writes 11% longer outputs and derails more in all six AIME configurations, although its offline error is the same. Whatever makes the difference, the averaged single-step error we measure does not see it. The calibration set would have rejected LM-c2 for Qwen3, but it favored LM-c2 on the R1 models by 2.5–3.3 pp, a gain that did not hold on the test sets. 5.8 Can derailed runs be rescued after the fact? Spending the bytes on more low-bit tokens, with the bit-width set by a short end-to-end calibration, beat eviction in 17 of 18 settings and matched a joint rate–distortion allocator that uses more memory. Offline attention error and per-head probes did not identify the bit-width, so we would not set it without an end-to-end run. The open problem is derailment on long traces. On Qwen3-8B, 40% of 2-bit runs at our tightest budget still reach the cap, and forcing a conclusion recovers few of them. If our account of derailment is right, a cache that keeps even a coarse record of what the model has already checked should help more than a better token scorer. Limitations Calibration. The calibration set is small and was validated at two budgets. At these budgets, always using 2 bits is statistically on par with calibration. The benefit of calibration is that it avoids the model-specific failures of other fixed choices; whether it is needed at larger budgets has not been tested on held-out data. Statistical power. AIME has 30 problems per year, so single-setting confidence intervals are wide. Cross-setting claims rest on pooled tests. Each configuration uses one sampling seed; variance across seeds is covered only through repeated samples per problem and is not reported separately. Models, tasks and languages. We study three open 7–8B reasoning models (two R1-distilled, one Qwen3) on English mathematics and science benchmarks; GPQA was run on one model only. We did not evaluate code generation, long-input tasks, other languages, larger models or other reasoning-model families, so the breadth–depth trade-off and the calibrated bit-widths may differ there. Mechanism. The derailment analysis is correlational, and the mechanism in § 5.6 is a hypothesis we have not tested. The rescue experiment used a literal-repetition detector, ran on calibration data only and intervened late. Reproduced baselines. RDKV’s decode mode has no total budget, so its memory is matched only approximately, and we modified the zero point of its quantizer (we also report as-released results). ThinKV has no public code; our re-implementation fixes details the paper leaves open, calibrates thresholds on runtime sparsity and adds K-channel centering, whose per-segment means our byte count only partly charges (we report a bound). Results from the authors’ own implementations may differ. Scope of the comparisons. The sub-2-bit study covers one codec family; vector or learned codebooks might move the floor. The low-rank baseline uses a frozen basis. We did not run every recent reasoning-specific method; R-KV represents reasoning-aware eviction. Simulated quantization. Quantization is simulated in the engine (quantize, then dequantize) with exact byte accounting. We do not measure end-to-end memory or serving throughput; the sequence counts in § 5.9 are a projection from the kernel, which uses a closely related but not identical layout. Test contamination. Some benchmarks, MATH500 in particular, may appear in the models’ training data. All comparisons are between compression methods on the same model, so contamination should affect absolute accuracy more than the differences we report, but we cannot rule out interactions. Ethical Considerations This work studies inference efficiency and poses low direct risk. Compression can preserve final answers while degrading the reasoning that supports them ( Ai et al., 2026 ) , so compressed reasoning models should be evaluated beyond final-answer accuracy before deployment. Each problem is sent as a single user turn through the model’s chat template (Qwen3 with thinking enabled), followed by “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{} .” For GPQA the suffix asks for the letter of the correct option (A–D) within \boxed{} ; each question lists its four options as lettered choices. Grading. We take the last \boxed{} after </think> (or anywhere in the output if the answer region has none). Math answers are compared with math-verify (0.9.0), falling back to exact string match after removing spaces; GPQA answers are compared by option letter. Runs that hit the length cap without an answer count as wrong. Data. MATH500 (500 problems), AIME 2024 and 2025 (30 each) and GPQA-Diamond (198) are loaded from Hugging Face copies. The calibration set is the 60 AIME 2022–2023 problems of the AIMO validation set, disjoint from all test sets. Engine and software. Models run in bf16 in our own decoding engine (FlashAttention-2 decode, CUDA graphs, per-head variable-length caches) with PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.56.2, FlashAttention 2.8.3 and Triton 3.4.0. Generation runs used H200 and A800 GPUs and took about 344 GPU-hours in total, excluding offline analyses. Eviction details. SnapKV-D scores decode tokens by the attention of the last 8 queries, max-pooled with kernel 7, and always keeps the 8 most recent tokens. All methods compress every 128 decode steps. Appendix B PACT: Per-Head Online Allocation PACT was our first attempt to choose the bit-width online, separately for each KV head. It is a negative result, and we report it here for completeness. Format and selection. PACT uses the hybrids’ K format, with V quantized per token in a Hadamard-rotated basis ( b + 0.25 b+0.25 bits); quantizing K per token gives a relative attention error of 1.92 at layer 0 at 2 bits, even after rotation. At each compression step, a head keeps its top- K b K_{b} tokens by attention from the last 32 queries, stored at b b bits, where K b K_{b} is the number of tokens the budget can hold at that width. Variants. PACT-B reads b b from a budget-indexed table chosen on the dev set (512 → \to 3, 1024 → \to 4, 2048 → \to 8). PACT-LA tries each b ∈ { 16 , 8 , 4 , 3 , 2 } b\in\{16,8,4,3,2\} that is not above the head’s current width, measures the relative change in the attention output of the last 32 queries (the probe), and picks the b b with the smallest change, evaluating each b b at the number of tokens it could keep once the history has grown by a factor of γ = 4 \gamma=4 . A head’s precision never increases. Without this look-ahead, the probe picks 8 bits for 88% of heads and inflates output lengths. Offline motivation. With per-token-independent quantization on the pilot traces, letting each head choose its own bit-width lowers attention error by 20–42% relative to the best single width shared by all heads, and a probe on the last 64 queries recovers 90–95% of this per-head oracle gain.
